title: Buying the Right Analyzer: Uptime, Throughput and Batch vs Random Access
summary: See why a STAT tube waits on a batch analyzer but not a random-access one, how vendors can inflate uptime, and how rerun rates and capacity math guide the “right buy”.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 2 Hits 8, 10–12 and Trap 3, plus the Number Vault rerun-rate (25% vs 20%) and capacity (2 × 500 vs 1 × 1,000) rows. Batch vs continuous access, marketed throughput and per-analyzer QC are checked externally; the uptime contract definition, breakthrough-technology economics and rerun example stay pending.

objectives: Distinguish batch from continuous random-access analyzers and predict what happens to a STAT sample on each.
Explain why the laboratory, not the vendor, should define instrument downtime.
Calculate a rerun rate and decide whether reruns call for new equipment or revised rules.
Weigh one large analyzer against two smaller ones for capacity, backup and QC workload.

scenes.title: The brochure vs the bad night
scenes.altText: A glossy vendor brochure promises “99% uptime” and “1,000 tests per hour”. Beside it, a lab night log reads: “Interface down 6 h — no results reported.” The cartoon scientist looks from one to the other, puzzled.

cues.text: The sales brochure promises 99 percent uptime and a thousand tests every hour.
But last night the lab could not report a single result for six hours — and the vendor still counts the analyzer as “up.”
How can both be true? And how should a lab choose, and judge, an instrument?

scenes.title: Batch vs random access
scenes.altText: Two analyzers side by side. Left, a batch analyzer: a rack of tubes loads, a door icon closes and the run starts; a red STAT tube arrives and waits outside until the run ends. Right, a continuous random-access analyzer: tubes join one at a time, and the STAT tube slides straight in. Labels: batch — cheaper per test, less timely; random access — timely, STAT-friendly.

cues.text: Analyzers handle tubes in two basic ways. A batch analyzer runs a whole set of samples together, as one run.
Once the run starts, the set is closed. New samples wait until it finishes.
So when an urgent STAT tube arrives mid-run, it has to wait.
A continuous, random-access analyzer accepts new samples at any time, even while it is running. The STAT tube goes straight in.
The trade-off the reviewer highlights: batching spreads controls and setup over many samples, so it is cheaper per test — but slower for any single urgent result.

scenes.title: What counts as “down”?
scenes.altText: A timeline of one day for one analyzer. A short red block marks a hardware fault. Longer amber blocks mark an interface outage and a QC failure waiting for service. Under the vendor’s narrow definition, only the red block counts as down (uptime near 99%). Under the laboratory’s definition — “if we cannot report patient results, it is down” — all blocks count and uptime drops. Then a throughput gauge: the brochure’s 1,000 tests per hour on an ideal mix falls to a lower number on the lab’s real test mix.

cues.text: Here is one analyzer’s day. A short hardware fault — the vendor counts that as down.
But the interface to the lab system also failed for hours, and a QC failure waited for service. No patient results went out.
The vendor’s narrow definition ignores those hours, so its uptime still looks near 99 percent.
The reviewer’s rule for the contract: if the lab cannot report patient results, the instrument is down. Count every one of those hours.
Throughput works the same way. Marketed speeds are only a ballpark estimate; real speed depends on your own test orders and volume. Measure with your own mix.

keys.label: Real test mix: measure it yourself

scenes.title: In the lab: reruns and the “right buy”
scenes.altText: Two analyzers each test 500 samples. Analyzer A reruns 125 (25%), mostly triggered by the lab’s own delta-check and critical-value rules. Analyzer B reruns 100 (20%), mostly from instrument flags. A wrench icon shows that A’s problem is fixed by revising delta-check limits, not by buying a new analyzer. Then two capacity options: two analyzers of 500 tests per hour versus one of 1,000 — same capacity on paper; the pair keeps testing if one is down, but each needs its own QC and maintenance.

cues.text: Rerun rate is the share of samples tested a second time. Analyzer A reran 125 of 500 samples: 125 divided by 500 is 25 percent.
Analyzer B reran 100 of 500: 20 percent. A looks worse.
But look at why. Most of A’s reruns were set off by the lab’s own rules — delta checks and critical values. Revising those limits cuts reruns without buying anything.
Now capacity. Two analyzers at 500 tests per hour, or one at 1,000? On paper, the same.
Two give a backup if one goes down; one means a single set of QC and maintenance. The right buy matches measured need — not overbuying, not underbuying.

props.label: Why: lab rules (delta check, critical value)

scenes.title: Traps: uptime, speed and shiny new tech
scenes.altText: A trap card “Vendor uptime is a reliable comparison number” is crossed out and replaced with “Define down as: cannot report results; measure throughput with your own mix”. Then a “breakthrough technology” card lists: changes workflow, consolidates workstations, premium price, early adopters pay more. A final pair contrasts batch (waits) with random access (any time).

cues.text: Trap: “The vendor’s uptime number is reliable for comparing instruments.” Not so — vendors can define “down” narrowly.
Write the contract so that “cannot report patient results” means down, and test throughput with your own test mix.
Breakthrough technology changes workflow and can merge workstations, but it costs a premium. The reviewer warns that early buyers often pay more and gain less than labs that wait.
And don’t swap the analyzers: batch means the run is closed until it ends; random access accepts a STAT any time.

scenes.title: Bus vs taxi · Down = can’t report
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a bus (batch) that leaves on schedule and lets no one board mid-route, beside a taxi (random access) that picks up a STAT passenger any time. A stamp reads “DOWN = CAN’T REPORT”. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid: a batch analyzer is a bus. Everyone boards, the doors close, and no one gets on until the next trip.
A random-access analyzer is a taxi: it picks up the urgent passenger right away. And for uptime, remember: down means can’t report.
Where it breaks: many modern analyzers mix both styles, and some batch systems have a STAT port. The bus picture also hides that batching can lower cost per test.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: A contract card reads “Down = can’t report results”, beside a bus and a taxi icon and a gauge labelled “your real test mix”.

cues.text: Judge an instrument by your own data — define down as “cannot report patient results,” measure throughput with your real test mix, and remember batch runs make STATs wait while random-access analyzers take them any time.

props.text: Batch makes STATs wait · random access takes them

explanation.what: Plain language: some analyzers run tubes in closed groups, others take tubes any time; and an instrument is only “up” if the lab can actually send results. Scientific terms: a batch analyzer tests a set of samples as one run and accepts a new set only after the run is complete, while a continuous (random-access) analyzer accepts new samples while running. Uptime is the share of time the instrument is available; the laboratory should define downtime as any time it cannot report patient results.
explanation.why: In a batch run the set is closed, so a STAT sample waits for the run to end; continuous access removes that wait. Batching spreads controls and setup over many samples, which can lower cost per test. Vendors may count only hardware failure as downtime, so interface outages or QC failures awaiting service vanish from their uptime figure. Marketed throughput depends on the actual test orders and sample volume, so it is only an estimate for your lab.
explanation.measure: Rerun rate = reruns ÷ samples tested (125 ÷ 500 = 25%). Uptime = hours able to report ÷ total hours. Throughput = tests completed per hour on the lab’s real mix. These numbers, not brochures, decide the “right buy”.
explanation.differs: Batch vs random access: closed run vs open any time. Vendor vs lab uptime: hardware-only vs “can’t report = down”. Rerun cause: lab rules (fix the rules) vs instrument flags (look at the instrument). 2 × 500 vs 1 × 1,000: backup vs single QC/maintenance load.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “A STAT arrives during a batch run — what happens?” (it waits), “How should uptime be defined in a contract?” (cannot report patient results = down), a rerun-rate calculation, and the trap that vendor uptime is reliable.

mnemonic.text: Batch = bus, random access = taxi; down = can’t report.
mnemonic.explanation: A bus closes its doors and leaves on a schedule — late passengers wait for the next trip, like a STAT on a batch run. A taxi picks up an urgent passenger at once. For uptime, if you can’t report, it’s down.
mnemonic.limitation: Many modern analyzers combine features, and some batch systems include a STAT port that shortens the wait. The bus picture hides that batching can lower cost per test, and the “down” rule is the reviewer’s recommendation for contracts, not a regulatory definition.

questions.stem: A STAT troponin arrives while a batch analyzer is in the middle of a run. What happens on a true batch system?

options.text: The STAT sample waits until the current run finishes
options.rationale: Correct. A batch run is a closed set; a new sample can enter only after the run is complete, which delays STATs.

options.text: The STAT sample is loaded immediately and tested next
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes a continuous random-access analyzer.

options.text: The run is cancelled and restarted with the STAT included
options.rationale: Incorrect. Batch runs are not normally interrupted; cancelling would waste the whole run.

options.text: The analyzer automatically sends the STAT to point-of-care testing
options.rationale: Incorrect. Analyzers do not reroute samples to bedside testing.

questions.stem: An analyzer tested 600 samples last week and 90 of them had to be rerun. What is the rerun rate?

options.rationale: Incorrect. This divides the samples by the reruns (600 ÷ 90 ≈ 6.7) and adds a percent sign.
Incorrect. 0.15 is the fraction; multiply by 100 to get 15%.
Incorrect. 85% is the share of samples that did NOT need a rerun.

questions.stem: When negotiating an analyzer contract, how should the laboratory define instrument downtime?

options.text: Any time the laboratory cannot report patient results from the instrument
options.rationale: Correct. This patient-centered definition captures interface outages, QC failures awaiting service and other gaps that a narrow definition hides.

options.text: Only the time the instrument hardware is broken
options.rationale: Incorrect. This narrow vendor-style definition makes uptime look better than the lab actually experiences.

options.text: Only the time a service engineer is on site
options.rationale: Incorrect. Waiting for the engineer is often the longest part of an outage, and this would exclude it.

options.text: The time the vendor’s brochure lists as scheduled maintenance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Brochure figures are not the lab’s experience; the contract should reflect real ability to report results.

claims.text: A batch analyzer tests a set of samples as one run; continuous random-access analyzers accept new samples while running.
On batch-style systems a STAT sample is delayed until samples already in process are completed.
Marketed throughput depends on actual test orders and sample volume and is only an estimate for a given laboratory.
Each separate analyzer requires its own QC and maintenance; a disabled single system can stop testing unless there is a backup.
Batching is cheaper per test but less timely than continuous random-access processing.
claims.note: Plausible (fixed QC/setup spread over more samples) but not stated in the sources consulted.

claims.text: Contracts should define the instrument as down whenever the laboratory cannot report patient results; vendors may use narrower definitions.
claims.note: Reviewer’s recommendation; no external source consulted states this contract wording.

claims.text: Breakthrough technology changes workflow, consolidates workstations and commands premium pricing; early adopters pay more and gain less.
125 ÷ 500 = 25%; 100 ÷ 500 = 20%; 90 ÷ 600 = 15%. Reruns driven by lab rules are reduced by revising delta-check limits.
claims.note: Arithmetic is correct; the scenario and the remedy are the reviewer’s worked example.

accuracyFlags.issue: The “cannot report = down” rule is a recommendation from the reviewer’s source, not a regulatory or standard definition; contract terms vary.
The reviewer says a batch analyzer “cannot be interrupted”; some batch-mode systems offer STAT ports or priority loading.
accuracyFlags.resolution: Lesson and memory aid note that many analyzers mix features and some batch systems have STAT ports.
